extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers of literature, and writers studying Vargas Llosa's style
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the recurring stylistic, thematic, and technical criteria the Wikipedia article attributes to Mario Vargas Llosa's fiction and non-fiction — useful for writers or analysts learning from his techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of historical material and personal experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Vargas Llosa's style 'encompasses historical material as well as his own experiences.' (e.g. The Time of the Hero informed by his experiences at Leoncio Prado military school).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor fiction in researched history or lived experience to lend authenticity and thematic resonance; use personal events as source material to depict institutions and social corruption. Examples: The Time of the Hero draws on his academy experience; The War of the End of the World draws on Euclides da Cunha's account of Canudos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploration of themes: corruption, oppression, individual's struggle for freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent themes include 'the individual's struggle for freedom within an oppressive reality', corruption of institutions, demoralization and political oppression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make social/political critique a central engine of plot and character motivation; show how institutions mirror or produce individual suffering. Works like Conversation in The Cathedral and The Green House exemplify this thematic focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance factual accuracy and fictional liberty in historical novels
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing historical novels Vargas Llosa said 'I respected the basic facts, ... I have not exaggerated' but also 'It's a novel, not a history book, so I took many, many liberties.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do careful historical research and 'respect basic facts' while accepting and signaling the novel's license to fictionalize; thorough preparation (comprehensive study of the subject's history) is expected for credibility (e.g., The Feast of the Goat).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modernist technical complexity and seriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Early works are described as having 'difficulty and technical complexity' and a 'certain seriousness of attitude' — elements of the modern novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ complex narrative structures, dense thematic layering, and a sober tone when aiming for modernist seriousness (examples: The Green House, Conversation in The Cathedral). Such complexity is treated as a mark of ambition and literary value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postmodernist, comic, and farcical modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Later novels 'appear to follow a postmodernist mode of writing' with 'a much lighter, farcical, and comic tone' (examples: Captain Pantoja and the Special Service, Aunt Julia and the Scriptwriter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Switching to lighter, metafictional, or parodic modes can be deliberate — use humor, popular-culture registers, and self-reflexivity to achieve postmodern effects; tonal shift should suit subject and intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlacing dialogues (weaving conversations to shift time/location)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technique of 'interlacing dialogues'—combining two conversations that occur at different times to create the illusion of a flashback or to shift location, used to weave together events separated in time/space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use juxtaposed dialogues as a device to create flashbacks, parallel actions, or spatial shifts. The technique can produce sober, serious effects (The Green House) or comic effects (Captain Pantoja) depending on execution. It is compared to mixing soliloquies (Woolf) and Flaubert's counterpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensive use of conversation as structural device
rubrics_metrics.description: Influenced by Sartre, Vargas Llosa makes 'extensive use of conversation' in his work; conversation often drives narrative and structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let dialogue carry plot, reveal character, and structure narrative momentum. Conversations may serve as long set pieces (e.g., the long bar conversation in Conversation in The Cathedral) and as a technique to explore ideas and power dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterpoint and blending of speech with events (Flaubertian technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technique likened to Flaubert's 'counterpoint' in which conversation is blended with other events, such as speeches; Vargas Llosa uses similar blending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine dialogue with narrative events or speeches to create contrapuntal texture; this blending can enrich narrative by layering perspectives and rhythmic contrasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and form shift across career (shorter novels, discovery of humor)
rubrics_metrics.description: After early ambitious novels, Vargas Llosa 'began to write novels that were significantly shorter' and entered a phase called 'the discovery of humor', moving into satirical and comic forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to adapt novel length and tone over a career to explore different registers; concision and comedic timing can be deliberate stylistic choices following earlier expansive works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of popular-culture language and imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Aunt Julia and the Scriptwriter is 'one of the most striking examples of how the language and imagery of popular culture can be used in literature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate popular media registers and imagery to enrich voice, create immediacy, or comment on mass culture; this can help novels connect to broader cultural speech and comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody and satirical reworking of earlier themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Captain Pantoja and the Special Service is described as 'essentially a parody of both The Green House and the literary approach that novel represents.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody can be used to revisit earlier themes from a new angle; using parody/satire allows critique of institutions or of literary modes themselves while reusing familiar material for comic ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of collective voice and shifting verb tenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Los cachorros uses a 'collective voice and shifting verb tenses' to treat adolescence, exclusion, and 'virilidad mutilada.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment with narrative person and tense to convey group experience or fractured identity; collective narration and tense shifts can emphasize social dynamics and psychological states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambition in scope: thematic breadth and political engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Vargas Llosa's works range across comedy, mystery, historical novel, political thriller; he 'wrote prolifically across various literary genres' and used fiction to 'challenge the inadequacies of society.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for thematic breadth if intending serious social criticism—novels can combine genres and scales (local experience to historical events) to interrogate power, fanaticism, and ideology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transforming historical figures into fiction requires narrative daring
rubrics_metrics.description: On The Way to Paradise (Flora Tristan and Paul Gauguin) critics argued Vargas Llosa 'was not as successful in transforming these historical figures into fiction' and lacked 'audacity, energy, political vision, and narrative genius.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When fictionalizing real figures, ensure strong narrative vision and imaginative energy; thorough research alone is insufficient—authorial audacity and storytelling craft are required to make biographical fiction compelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of predecessor techniques (Faulkner, Flaubert, Sartre) on narrative time and form
rubrics_metrics.description: Vargas Llosa admired Faulkner for 'intricate changes in time and narration' and Flaubert and Sartre influenced his mixing of dialogues and conversation-centered structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study and selectively adapt narrative experiments from predecessors (complex chronology, soliloquy mixing, counterpoint) to shape time, perspective, and voice in one's own work; technical inheritance can inform but should be reworked creatively.
